question: Which multi-objective, risk-sensitive, and environment-modal task preferences cannot be represented by a single scalar Markov reward while preserving the full ordering over policies or trajectories, and can those tasks nevertheless be learned by bespoke reinforcement-learning algorithms?

key_findings.claim: The draft argues that scalarizing a multi-objective MDP without changing its complete policy ordering is possible only through a linear combination of the component rewards.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 represents each policy by its discounted state-action occupancy vector and each expected return by a linear functional of that vector. It concludes that any scalar reward whose policy ordering is determined by the component evaluation functions must itself induce a weighted sum of those evaluations; Corollaries 2-5 then rule out nondegenerate LexMax, MaxMin, MaxSat, and constrained-satisfaction objectives.

key_findings.claim: The ICLR draft's proof of the linear-scalarization theorem omits a necessary extension step that the authors later supplied in the UAI 2023 supplementary proof.
key_findings.evidence: On page 4 the draft moves from agreement on occupancy vectors realized by policies to the assertion that the intervening map must be linear, without establishing that the realized occupancy image is rich enough for that conclusion. The later UAI supplement introduces the smallest affine occupancy subspace, invokes openness of the occupancy image in that subspace, and explicitly extends equality from realized occupancies to the whole subspace before deriving the linear combination. The later proof supports the intended result, but those ingredients are absent from this reviewed revision.

key_findings.claim: The draft's ConSat impossibility theorem is false as written because it omits the case in which every policy satisfies the constraint.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5 permits scalarization only when the two rewards are equivalent or when max_pi J1(pi) is at most c. If instead min_pi J1(pi) is at least c, Definition 5 orders every policy solely by J2, so R2 is an immediate scalarization. The published UAI version adds exactly this missing exception, confirming that the submission statement was incomplete.

key_findings.claim: For an environment-agnostic exact transformation of all coherent trajectory returns, the standard exponential, isoelastic, logarithmic, and quadratic risk-averse utilities cannot themselves be represented by another nonconstant scalar Markov reward.
key_findings.evidence: Lemmas 1-3 show that a Markov reward for f(G1) would have to assign the same immediate transition reward for at least three distinct continuation returns. For each named nonlinear utility, the relevant one-dimensional expression has at most two preimages under the stated injectivity/domain assumptions, producing a contradiction. The quantification is over every coherent trajectory rather than only trajectories reachable in one known MDP.

anchors.section: 3 Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning / Lemmas 1-3 and Theorems 6-7

key_findings.claim: A nontrivial modal task can be converted to an ordinary reward after fixing and fully knowing an environment, but no single environment-independent Markov reward preserves that task across all transition functions.
key_findings.evidence: The modal reward is allowed to depend on the transition function, capturing requirements such as preserving the ability to return to the start or reach a shutdown control. For a fixed transition function one can set R equal to the induced modal reward. Robust equivalence across all transition functions exists only for modal rewards defined as trivial, making the second half of Theorem 10 definitional but clarifying the task-environment coupling.

key_findings.claim: The paper establishes expressivity separations, not that the inexpressible objectives are unlearnable, and its proposed general solvers remain unimplemented sketches.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 points to existing specialized algorithms and proposes differentiating a smooth utility U(J1,...,Jk) for general MORL. Appendix E sketches k off-policy affordance Q-functions whose estimated optimal values feed a modal reward and a separate task Q-function. It gives no experiment, sample-complexity result, function-approximation guarantee, or implemented comparison; even tabular convergence is left to a prospective proof.

anchors.section: Appendix E, convergence and exploration discussion

method.core_idea: Treat a task as a complete preference ordering rather than merely a desired optimum, then use linear occupancy geometry and trajectory-continuation arguments to test whether scalar Markov rewards can represent three broader objective classes.
method.mechanism: For multi-objective tasks, expected component returns and a candidate scalar return are linear functionals of discounted occupancy measures, constraining exact scalarizations to weighted sums. For nonlinear risk utilities, decomposing a trajectory into one transition plus a continuation imposes functional equations that ordinary rewards cannot satisfy. For modal tasks, allowing the objective to inspect environment dynamics exposes the difference between a reward constructed for one known transition model and a portable task specification. The paper then sketches gradient-based MORL and multi-Q affordance learners as alternatives.
assumptions: Task equivalence means preserving the full strict ordering over all policies, not only sharing an optimal policy or acceptable-policy set.
Policies are stationary in a finite-state, finite-action discounted MDP and ordinary rewards are scalar functions of the current state, action, and next state.
The risk-sensitive impossibility analysis requires exact equality G2(xi)=f(G1(xi)) for every coherent trajectory, including trajectories an individual environment may never realize.
The named risk utilities satisfy the paper's nonconstancy, injectivity, parameter, and domain restrictions.
Robust modal expressivity is judged using one fixed reward across every possible transition function over the state-action space.
The proposed modal learner can estimate every affordance's optimal value off-policy with sufficient exploration and suitable learning rates.

techniques.role: Defines successful expression as preserving preferences among suboptimal as well as optimal policies.
Represents policy returns as linear functionals of state-action occupancy vectors to constrain scalarization.
Tests whether a nonlinear transformation of return can decompose into Markovian one-step rewards.
Lets task value depend on transition dynamics and distinguishes contingent from robust equivalence.
Sketches direct optimization of differentiable multi-objective aggregators without scalar Markov reduction.
Sketches modal learning by estimating auxiliary optimal-value functions and feeding them into the task objective.

evaluations.setting: Finite discounted multi-objective MDPs evaluated by complete policy orderings.
evaluations.metric: Existence of a scalar Markov reward inducing exactly the same policy order.
evaluations.result: The draft claims scalarizability only via a linear weighting and derives generic impossibility results for LexMax, MaxMin, MaxSat, and ConSat; the ConSat statement requires the additional all-policies-feasible exception added in the published version.
evaluations.baseline: Direct multi-objective evaluation functions versus a single scalar Markov reward on the same state, action, dynamics, start distribution, and discount.

evaluations.setting: All coherent infinite trajectories under a nonconstant base reward and standard nonlinear risk utilities.
evaluations.metric: Existence of a Markov reward whose return equals the transformed base return on every trajectory.
evaluations.result: No such reward exists for the exponential, isoelastic, logarithmic, or restricted quadratic transformations under the stated conditions.
evaluations.baseline: The original Markov return and linear/degenerate transformations for which one-step decomposition is not ruled out.

evaluations.setting: Modal rewards whose values may depend on the environment transition function.
evaluations.metric: Contingent equivalence in one fixed environment versus robust equivalence across all transition functions.
evaluations.result: Every modal task has a contingent ordinary reward once the transition function is fixed; by definition, only trivial modal rewards have one ordinary reward that is robustly equivalent across environments.

limitations: Author-stated: the paper does not give a general necessary-and-sufficient characterization of all policy orderings representable by reward functions; Appendix B provides only initial properties.
Author-stated: the risk analysis does not characterize every function f for which a transformed return can be represented by another reward.
Author-stated: the general MORL and affordance-based modal algorithms are sketches; implementation, evaluation, and even the modal method's formal tabular convergence proof are left to future work.

Reviewer-identified: the reviewed ICLR draft's main MORL proof skips the occupancy-image openness/extension argument later added in the UAI supplement, so page 4 alone does not establish its stated conclusion.
Reviewer-identified: draft Theorem 5 omits the min_pi J1(pi)>=c case, where every policy is feasible and R2 trivially represents ConSat; the published version corrects this.

Reviewer-identified: exact transformation of all coherent trajectory returns is substantially stronger than representing a risk preference in one fixed MDP, so the risk theorems should not be read as excluding every scalar treatment of risk-sensitive behavior.

Reviewer-identified: expressivity depends on what is included in the state. History augmentation, automata, belief state, learned world state, or transition-dependent discounting can turn some apparently non-Markovian specifications into Markovian ones in a larger formalism.

Reviewer-identified: robust modal non-equivalence follows immediately from the definition of a nontrivial modal reward; the substantive open issue is the cost and learnability of portable modal specifications, which the paper does not measure.
failure_modes: Using only shared optimal policies as the comparison criterion can erase the paper's separations, because many otherwise inexpressible orderings admit a reward with the same optimum.
Constraining attention to a single known transition graph can make a nonlinear risk or modal task contingently representable even when the environment-agnostic theorem rules it out.
A purported scalarization may work on sampled policies while reversing untested suboptimal-policy comparisons, failing the paper's global equivalence criterion.
Affordance estimates can be wrong in poorly explored states, corrupting the derived modal reward precisely where reachability or shutdown guarantees matter.
Jointly changing the state representation and reward formalism can make an expressivity comparison appear to favor rewards even though memory was moved into the state.
Smooth surrogates for LexMax, MaxMin, or MaxSat can be optimizable but need not preserve the sharp objective's exact ordering or constraints.
reusable_insights: Specify what equivalence must preserve—optimal set, acceptable set, trajectory order, or full policy order—before claiming that one objective formalism subsumes another.
Occupancy measures turn many reward-expressivity questions into questions about which linear functionals or nonlinear outer functions are available on the realizable occupancy set.
Separate objective representation from objective optimization: failure of Markov scalarization does not imply failure of RL-like learning.
Test portability across dynamics when a task refers to affordances such as reversibility, shutdown access, or future reachability.
When a proof reasons from realized policies to an ambient vector space, explicitly establish span, affine-hull, or relative-openness conditions before extending a functional identity.
Audit degenerate boundary cases—especially always-satisfied and never-satisfied constraints—before presenting an impossibility theorem.
open_questions: What intuitive axioms exactly characterize the policy orderings representable by scalar Markov rewards under fixed versus variable state representations?
Which nonlinear transformations f admit an exact Markovian return decomposition, and how does the answer change when only reachable trajectories in a fixed MDP matter?
Can a practical affordance learner estimate modal safety predicates with calibrated uncertainty and finite-sample guarantees before deployment?
How should objective-specification formalisms be compared jointly on expressivity, learnability, sample complexity, compositionality, and robustness to dynamics shift?
Can reward or preference learning infer outer nonlinear, multi-objective, temporal-logic, or modal objectives without forcing them through a Markov scalar bottleneck?
Which conclusions survive partial observability, continuous spaces, nonstationary policies, learned state abstractions, and transition-dependent discount factors?

competitive_landscape.title: On the Expressivity of Markov Reward
competitive_landscape.difference: Abel et al. formalize tasks as acceptable-policy sets, policy orderings, or trajectory orderings and give counterexamples plus linear-program constructions. This draft adopts the policy-order view but targets broad multi-objective, nonlinear-risk, and modal families rather than isolated existence examples.

competitive_landscape.title: Scalar Reward Is Not Enough: A Response to Silver, Singh, Precup and Sutton (2021)
competitive_landscape.difference: Vamplew et al. argue conceptually, biologically, and from safety considerations for explicitly multi-objective intelligence. The reviewed paper narrows the claim to formal policy-order scalarizability and supplies mathematical separations rather than a general AGI position argument.

competitive_landscape.title: Settling the Reward Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.difference: Bowling et al. characterize when preferences over distributions of histories admit a recursively decomposable reward and transition-dependent discount under explicit axioms. Its conditional positive theorem and broader discount formalism clarify why the reviewed draft's categorical workshop title overstates a result tied to fixed Markov rewards and its chosen task semantics.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Expressivity of Objective-Specification Formalisms in Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Subramani et al. compare 17 formalisms in an expressivity preorder and show several—including reward machines, temporal logic, regularized RL, and nonlinear Markov objectives—are mutually incomparable. It generalizes beyond the reviewed paper's three task classes and turns alternative formalisms into the central object of analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Reward Machines: Exploiting Reward Function Structure in Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Icarte et al. use finite-state reward machines to specify regular-language, temporally extended objectives and provide concrete tabular and continuous-control learning methods. Reward machines address history dependence constructively but do not dominate arbitrary nonlinear policy-order or environment-modal objectives.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims broad impossibility results for scalar Markov rewards across multi-objective, risk-sensitive, and newly formalized modal tasks, together with necessary-and-sufficient multi-objective scalarization conditions and sketches showing that inexpressibility need not prevent learning.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The 16-page draft develops occupancy-based and continuation-based theorems, introduces modal rewards that inspect dynamics, and outlines smooth-utility and affordance-based learners. The same authors later published a repaired and retitled version at UAI 2023.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The class-level mathematical treatment and modal-task framing materially extend the closest 2021 expressivity work. Novelty should nevertheless be credited to the corrected UAI lineage, not to every statement in this draft: its main proof omits an extension lemma, its ConSat theorem misses a counterexample, and its algorithmic claims are unevaluated. Later ICLR 2024 work substantially broadens the formalism comparison.

reviewer_notes: Read all 16 cached pages and visually inspected every rendered page because extraction diagnostics warned about rotated text. All pages are portrait/upright with PDF rotation metadata 0; no rotated body text, hidden sideways theorem, or unreadable figure was found. The collection title 'THE REWARD HYPOTHESIS IS FALSE' corresponds to the authors' shorter NeurIPS 2022 ML Safety Workshop version. The exact-ID ICLR PDF reviewed here is titled 'Three Problem Classes That Markov Rewards Cannot Express.' The same Joar Skalse–Alessandro Abate work was subsequently corrected, expanded, and published at UAI 2023 as 'On the Limitations of Markovian Rewards to Express Multi-Objective, Risk-Sensitive, and Modal Tasks' (PMLR 216:1974-1984); that lineage was used only to audit the draft's proof and boundary cases, while all finding anchors point to the exact cached submission.
